content:
[1] Earlier this year, I swapped a petrol mower for a robotic mower that can be controlled with an iPhone. Users can manually drive the robot along the edges of the lawn to build a virtual map. Once set up, the robot will mow automatically on a preset schedule.

[1] Recently, I tested another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I think for many people this machine may be easier to use.

[2] Camera-assisted automatic mapping

[3] The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9, which I reviewed earlier this year, is how each understands your lawn.

[4] The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to first steer the mower along the boundary with my phone before it could build an initial map.

[5] The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the maker calls TerraVision 2.0. The mower is equipped with three cameras that can automatically map out the lawn area, with no boundary wire buried in the ground and no extra RTK antenna required.

[6] The automatic initial mapping process takes longer, but I think for people who aren't very familiar with computer technology it may be simpler.

[7] To verify this, I asked my mother, who lives in another US state, to set up and use the TerraMow V1000 entirely on her own, without any help from me. She said everything worked fine. That said, though, I'm not sure she would have had the patience to first steer the robot along the entire boundary with her phone and then mark out all the areas to avoid.

[8] During automatic mapping in the front yard, a few minor issues came up. There's no fence or other physical barrier between my lawn and my neighbour's grass, so TerraMow initially included part of the neighbour's lawn in my map.

[9] I set that area as a no-go zone in the app and the problem was solved right away. That said, if there's no clearly visible boundary between two lawns, you need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping.

[10] Viewing through the mower's cameras

[11] TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a real-time view of what the mower sees while it's working.

[12] During testing, I used iPhone's screen-mirroring feature to cast that video onto my Mac's big screen. I could sit indoors working while watching the mower move around the backyard from its own point of view.

[13] This feature isn't necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more fun, and sometimes explains why the mower slows down or avoids certain objects. The Anthbot M9 doesn't have an equivalent real-time camera view.

[14] Apart from that, the two iPhone apps share many common features. Both support preset schedules, mowing-mode adjustments, zone settings, no-go markers and remote control of the mower.

[15] Speaking of that last feature, TerraMow's design is quite thoughtful. Besides the traditional left/right virtual joysticks, its app also offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold the iPhone normally and steer the mower with your thumb.

[16] Manually driving the mower with an iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally the robot should run automatically on a preset schedule with no human intervention. Still, TerraMow's joystick mode is handy for tidying the small patches a robot mower may miss.

[17] Sometimes I almost felt as if I were controlling the robot by telekinesis (in that fun way). I'd walk behind the mower holding the iPhone, give it a little nudge with my thumb, and it would steer precisely to where I directed.

[18] Every robot mower app should copy this design.

[19] A more aggressive mower

[20] The TerraMow V1000 feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. During testing it cut closer to the ground and was noticeably louder when running.

[21] I wouldn't call the TerraMow "very loud," but the difference is obvious. The Anthbot runs very quietly — even when it's out at night with its headlights on, you can almost forget it's still going.

[22] Because TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to work reliably. So scheduling mowing during the day becomes more important.

[23] The V1000 feels solidly built and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective carport that covers the charging dock in the box, whereas Anthbot's carport has to be bought separately.

[24] Most importantly, the TerraMow has performed reliably the whole time. I've let it mow every day for several weeks on end and never needed any manual intervention.

[25] When adaptive mapping gets a bit "too clever"

[26] The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up sometimes backfires.

[27] The mower continually revises the map based on what it sees and hears. Saving those changes after each job takes quite a long time, during which you can't do anything in the app.

[28] After several days of heavy rain, I ran into an interesting extreme case. Water pooled in one spot in the yard, and TerraMow sensibly avoided that area on its next run.

[29] Inside the skipped circular patch, the weeds grew taller and taller. After a while the mower seemed to mistake the taller weeds there for something to avoid permanently, so even after the ground had dried the area kept being skipped.

[30] I used the remote-control function in the app to steer the mower over there manually and cut down the taller weeds, and the problem was resolved. Once the area was back to normal, automatic mowing resumed there too.

[31] Regular trimming along the edges also helps TerraMow get closer to the boundary with more confidence. Otherwise, taller weeds near the edge may be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

[32] Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. That method requires more preparation, but avoids the situation where the map "changes its mind" about the same patch of grass.

[33] 9to5Mac conclusion

[34] Having used both systems, for most people I'd lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-led approach.

[35] For me, burying a wire in the ground is completely out of the question, and installing an RTK base station means putting extra hardware somewhere, powering it and maintaining it. TerraMow needs neither.

[36] Its visual navigation isn't perfect. The initial mapping takes longer, fuzzy boundaries need manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook a weed-choked patch for a permanent obstacle.

[37] All of these issues are manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers easier setup, reliable automatic mowing, an attractive real-time camera view and the best manual-control experience of any robot mower app I've used.

[38] I do enjoy gardening, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing that chore over to a robot frees up time to look after flower beds, trim edges and do the detail work, while keeping the lawn tidy.

[39] The TerraMow V1000 shines in this regard, and I'd recommend it, especially for anyone who wants a robotic mower but doesn't want to bury wires, install an RTK antenna or walk the entire yard holding a phone from start to finish.

[40] Amazon currently prices the TerraMow V1000 at $999, with a $200 coupon code available on coupon sites. The product can also be purchased through TerraMow's official website.
